purpose: Post-attempt support after protected first answer is saved; no machine-diagnosis or independent QRT admission
hints_policy: H1 CLARIFY, H2 CORRELATE, H3 OPEN_THE_WAY; candidate texts require separate protected-W content review. All hints remain locked until first answer persists in the current runtime.

hints.H1: Separate the completed circular segment from the straight stage and declare the rail clock.
hints.H2: Recover the rail calibration and the signed velocity-area relation under constant acceleration.
hints.H3: Compare both rail position laws on the valid interval; distinguish whole-journey path and endpoint.

cycles.boundary_solution: At t=0 gap 12 m; at t=4 B=8 m and A=2π+8>8. The separation changes continuously and strictly decreases (closing speed π/2+t+1>0), so there is exactly one crossing within 0<t<4. No constant-average model is required.

hints.H1: Use one global time axis but reset elapsed time in the rail equation.
hints.H2: Find circular tangent speed before constructing the signed rail position and velocity laws.
hints.H3: Keep ground, scale and observer coordinates in distinct columns and verify both signed area sums.

cycles.boundary_solution: Relative positions at t=6,8,10 become 2,π+2,2 m; relative velocities +π,0,−π m/s. Relative displacement zero, as in ground. Rail and loop paths and whole-trip averages remain unchanged.

hints.H1: Identify the circular distance, period and initial tangent velocity separately from the rail measurements.
hints.H2: Use the odometer only as a signed displacement after checking the no-reversal condition.
hints.H3: Recover the acceleration, then compare both rail position laws and verify the endpoint using a velocity graph.

cycles.boundary_solution: At s=4 B is 2 m east of A. The gap decreases strictly throughout, so it never reaches zero in 0≤s≤4. A meeting after that cannot be asserted without later motion information.

hints.H1: Notice which values describe physical metres and which are logger divisions.
hints.H2: Compare the change between two common marks before considering the third report.
hints.H3: Write a candidate calibration and test a measurement that was not used to construct it.

cycles.boundary_solution: All three reports fit x=22−2r. This is evidence of consistency at these marks, not proof of uniform spacing everywhere.

hints.H2: Translate every reading to a common physical position before building the second table.
hints.H3: Keep the times aligned and check which signs change when the coordinate convention changes.

cycles.boundary_solution: B′=x−12 gives −10,−2,−2,−8 divisions. The signs reverse relative to B; the physical path and stationary interval are unchanged.

hints.H1: Separate the physical displacement from the numbers recorded by the two scales.
hints.H2: Use the two shared markers to relate the unknown scale to physical metres.
hints.H3: Recover the start first, then apply the signed physical change and invert both maps.

cycles.boundary_solution: Final x=16 m; P=22/3 divisions, Q=−1 division. Negative Q is a valid extrapolated coordinate if the uniform scale extends that far.

hints.H1: Identify which positions are actually observed and which intermediate positions remain unknown.
hints.H2: Compare the shortest route between successive checkpoint pairs with a route containing a detour.
hints.H3: Use an explicit list of possible turning positions to test the supervisor's assertion.

cycles.boundary_solution: Then D=9+4=13 m exactly and Δx=+5 m. The 19 m claim requires an extra reversal and contradicts the new condition.

hints.H1: Distinguish the absolute odometer reading from distance accumulated after A.
hints.H2: Recover each interval length from neighbouring odometer readings, then use its reported direction.
hints.H3: Align position and cumulative distance by checkpoint; inspect the signs of consecutive positions.

cycles.boundary_solution: Last change becomes +6 m, so final position is +12 m and displacement +9 m. Cumulative distance remains 25 m because odometer changes are unchanged.

hints.H1: Mark the direction order and the known second turn on a number line.
hints.H2: Write each leg length with the sign implied by its direction, keeping P unknown.
hints.H3: Use the measured total and then verify the recovered turning point against the assumed ordering.

cycles.boundary_solution: The formal equation 2P+6=8 gives P=1 m, making the westward leg zero. Strictly monotone nonzero legs require P>1, so D>8 m; a total of 8 m is impossible under these conditions.

hints.H1: Separate the measured endpoints from any assumption about the intervals between them.
hints.H2: Use the same endpoints to draw two continuous histories and compare their slopes.
hints.H3: Test which claims remain true under both histories, including existence rather than timing.

cycles.boundary_solution: Then v=−6+2t everywhere in the interval, zero uniquely at 3 s; acceleration is +2 m/s².

hints.H1: Name the quantity and units on each original and proposed graph axis.
hints.H2: Compute each slope and locate the times when the velocity changes sign.
hints.H3: Construct a time-aligned sign table without treating a negative velocity as negative speed.

cycles.boundary_solution: Acceleration signs become −3,0,+2 m/s²; velocity signs reverse as coordinate components, but physical directions and all speed-change intervals stay the same.

hints.H1: Use the total time to express the duration of the second acceleration stage.
hints.H2: Connect the change in velocity over each stage to its duration.
hints.H3: After recovering the switch, examine both velocity laws and test every zero against its own interval.

cycles.boundary_solution: −13+4τ=−5 gives τ=2 s. v(2)=+1 m/s; first zero at 5/3 s, second at 3 s. It reverses twice; final speed 5 m/s.

hints.H1: Identify the interval over which the acceleration is certified constant.
hints.H2: Choose a relation that retains time and then compare the velocity signs.
hints.H3: Test all candidate roots against the controller-change time and the original position law.

cycles.boundary_solution: Both t=2 and t=6 s are now inside the interval, with velocities +6 and −6 m/s respectively. Both cross the same point; only the first moves east.

hints.H1: Use one clock and mark the time where the acceleration law changes.
hints.H2: Find the velocity zero and the position at both the turn and the stage boundary.
hints.H3: Join the two graphs continuously and compare signed area with the magnitude-based route length.

cycles.boundary_solution: First stage unchanged; extend v=+3 to t=7, x=2+3(t−3), final x=14 m. Net Δx=+12 m and D=16.5 m.

hints.H1: Write the position law at each observation with one common start and acceleration.
hints.H2: Use both measurements to eliminate one unknown, then check the velocity law.
hints.H3: Locate any zero velocity before interpreting total distance; test the final stage conditions.

cycles.boundary_solution: The first 6 s are unchanged, then x=27 m stays constant. Displacement +27 m and distance 27 m. Applying the old constant acceleration after stopping would contradict the changed model.

hints.H1: Distinguish a location after a half revolution from the actual number of revolutions made.
hints.H2: Use the speed bounds to restrict how many additional full laps could have occurred.

cycles.boundary_solution: Yes, with T=18 s and speed 2π/3 m/s. The third observation is at 3/4 revolution. The first nine-second averages are unchanged.

hints.H1: Declare the compass axes and travel direction before making the table.
hints.H2: Advance one quarter revolution per five seconds and place each tangent perpendicular to its radius.
hints.H3: Compare cumulative distance with endpoint differences for each requested time window.

cycles.boundary_solution: Positions south,east,north,west,south,east; tangents east,north,west,south,east,north. Arc distances stay the same. From 0 to15 displacement (−5,+5) m; average velocity (−1/3,+1/3) m/s.

hints.H1: Use circumference as the distance for one full revolution, not π alone.
hints.H2: Find the total turn count and keep the fractional part when locating the endpoint.
hints.H3: Combine elapsed time, turn count and endpoint-vector change; verify the tangent using the direction of travel.

cycles.boundary_solution: 20π/(16π)=1.25 laps, T=18/1.25=14.4 s. Starting north, the quarter-lap remainder ends west (−8,0); tangent south. Average velocity (−4/9,−4/9) m/s.

cycles.boundary_solution: Remaining area 8 m=2(4+V), so V=0. The cart reaches zero only at t=6; it never moves west during the stated interval. Distance equals displacement 16 m.

cycles.boundary_solution: Its shore velocity is +2 m/s versus +3 for the kayak, so separation increases at 1 m/s. Water-frame difference is also −1 m/s; no future overtaking.

hints.H2: Subtract observer position at each shared time and derive slopes in the two frames.

hints.H2: Write the moving model from its actual boundary position, not a fictitious t=0 departure.

cycles.boundary_solution: B stays at x=30 for both stages. Substituting zero into the general delayed model xB=30−v(t−2) gives xB=30 and t=7.5 s, which is valid after t=2. This limit is legitimate; do not substitute into an already simplified expression that assumed v=3.
